extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, district-court judges, and appellate counsel involved in § 285 fee motions
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factors for determining whether a patent case is "exceptional" under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and for appellate review of a district court's fee award. Covers substantive-strength and litigation-conduct considerations, appellate forfeiture, and related evidentiary points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of appellate review for § 285 awards
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court’s award of attorney fees under § 285 is reviewed for an abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abuse of discretion occurs when the district court made a clear error of judgment in weighing relevant factors or based its decision on an error of law or clearly erroneous factual findings (Highmark Inc. v. Allcare Health Mgmt. Sys., Inc.; Bayer CropScience AG v. Dow AgroSciences LLC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory baseline — Section 285
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 285: 'The court in exceptional cases may award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute is discretionary; fees are available only in 'exceptional' cases. The determination is fact-intensive and committed to the district court's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'exceptional case' (Octane Fitness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An exceptional case 'is simply one that stands out from others with respect to the substantive strength of a party’s litigating position (considering both the governing law and the facts of the case) or the unreasonable manner in which the case was litigated.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Octane Fitness standard emphasizes the totality of circumstances and allows district courts broad discretion in determining exceptionality; the inquiry is rooted in factual determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-circumstances approach
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts consider the totality of the circumstances when deciding whether a case is exceptional under § 285.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may weigh multiple factors (e.g., pattern of litigation, weakness of claims, litigation conduct) collectively rather than requiring any single factor to be dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive strength of the litigating position
rubrics_metrics.description: A party’s substantive strength on the merits (both law and facts) is relevant to exceptionality; extremely weak positions can support fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even given the presumption of patent validity, a patent or claim that is 'demonstrably weak on its face' can justify fee awards. Specific untenable positions taken after a motion to dismiss (e.g., relying on arguments that case law rejects) weigh against the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Demonstrably weak on its face' patent criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be described as 'demonstrably weak on its face' such that no reasonable litigant could have expected success on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will consider the content of the claims and legal precedent (e.g., abstractness under § 101) and may find the patent weak despite issuance and the presumption of validity if positions advanced are untenable under controlling law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of frivolous litigation / litigation abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern of litigation abuses—characterized by repeated filing of patent infringement actions for the sole purpose of forcing settlements with no intention to test the merits—is relevant to an exceptional-case determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may include: high volume of suits (including suits involving the same patent), 'brief and boilerplate' complaints lacking particularized allegations, average settlement amounts, and other indicia that suits were filed to extract settlements (citing Eon-Net and SFA Sys.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation conduct (unreasonable/impolite/unprofessional conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreasonable or unprofessional litigation conduct by a party or its counsel is a proper factor in deciding exceptionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include threatening or coercive settlement communications and other conduct that, while not independently sanctionable, is nonetheless sufficiently 'unreasonable' to weigh in favor of fees (Octane Fitness: conduct need not be independently sanctionable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of counsel's conduct to the party
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may attribute counsel’s communications and conduct to the client for purposes of the § 285 inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emails or conduct by counsel showing settlement or litigation tactics can be imputed to the client and used as part of the factual record supporting exceptionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of patent validity considered but not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption of validity from PTO issuance is a factor but does not preclude a finding that a patent is 'demonstrably weak on its face.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will acknowledge the initial presumption but may nonetheless conclude that, in light of the claims and precedent, the patent lacks substantive strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of appellate arguments not raised below
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments or objections not presented to the district court are forfeited on appeal absent exceptional circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A position not presented in the tribunal below will not be considered on appeal unless exceptional circumstances justify review (In re Google Tech. Holdings). Lack of district-court objection (including consent to sealing) forecloses raising the issue for the first time on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-practicing entity status not alone dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: A party’s status as a non-practicing entity (NPE) is not by itself an appropriate basis for finding a case exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should rely on specific evidence of abusive filing practices rather than generalizations about NPEs; a generalization about an entity's status cannot serve as the sole basis for an exceptional-case finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scope of fee awards
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may limit the award of fees to the period from which the case became exceptional (e.g., from filing of a dispositive motion onward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court may choose a start point for fee liability (here, beginning when the defendant filed its motion to dismiss) based on when the record made clear the case was exceptionally weak or being litigated unreasonably.
